text:
Baby Atticus was just four weeks old(Image: Jam Press/Avon & Somerset Police)

A vicious father who "lost his temper" and violently shook his four-week-old baby to death has been jailed for life after he was found guilty of murder.

Tony Bartlett, 39, had drunk 8.5 pints on a night out before returning home and becoming "enraged" that his son Atticus was bringing up milk as he fed from a bottle.

Sentencing him to a minimum of 18 years in prison, sentencing judge Mr Justice Cavanagh said Bartlett had shaken his child "very violently indeed, gripping him very tightly round his ribcage".

Bartlett, of Axminster in Devon, inflicted severe injuries on Atticus in a moment of "pure violence" when he shook him at the family home in Chard, Somerset on July 16, 2022, a trial at Bristol Crown Court had previously heard.

Tony Bartlett was 'enraged' by Atticus’s inability to take the bottle as well as he thought the baby should(Image: Avon and Somerset Constabulary/PA Wire)

During the trial, Charles Row KC said Bartlett had been "drunk and frustrated" when he attacked his newborn son after he and his then-partner, Evelyn Ballentyne, Atticus's mother, had gone out to a pub and comedy club.

Ms Ballentyne's mother Rachel Donovan and her husband went to the family's home on Darcis Row to care for Atticus. Over the evening, Bartlett drank 8.5 pints of lager before returning home with Ms Ballentyne.

Bartlett had been feeding Atticus with a bottle and the baby was bringing up the milk, which the court heard had "enraged" him. The baby suffered severe internal injuries to the brain and spinal cord when he was violently shaken.

During sentencing, Mr Justice Cavanagh told the former postman he was "very drunk" when he carried out his fatal attack on Atticus. The judge said: "I have no doubt that this terrible tragedy would not have happened if you were not so heavily intoxicated."

Video grab of Tony Bartlett speaking with the police(Image: Avon and Somerset Police / SWNS)

Judge Cavanagh added: "In your drunken state, Atticus’s inability to take the bottle as well as you thought he should enraged you. You had a sudden fit of anger. You vented that anger on your tiny baby son.

"You shook him very violently indeed, gripping him very tightly round his ribcage. This only lasted a few seconds or at most a minute or so.

"Just in that brief moment, you wanted to cause Atticus serious injury. As suddenly as you began, you stopped, your anger evaporated, and then you dozed off."

During the trial, Mr Row told the court that Ms Ballentyne went upstairs "for a few minutes", leaving Atticus in Bartlett's sole care. The lawyer said: "When she returned, Atticus was lying face down across the defendant’s lap.

"She said 'he’s dead, he’s not breathing'. She noted that the defendant appeared to be asleep or at least his eyes were closed.

"The defendant flipped Atticus over. Atticus released two gasps and appeared to be floppy and lifeless."

Atticus was taken to Musgrove Park Hospital by emergency services before he was transferred to Bristol Royal Hospital for Children. His brain damage was so severe he did not regain consciousness or breathe for himself.

Atticus died just before midnight on July 23, 2022. Experts said the injuries suffered by Atticus were associated with "vigorous shaking", with his rib fractures caused by "gripping and squeezing" during that attack, Mr Row told the court.

Tony Bartlett arriving at Bristol Crown Court in June this year(Image: Ben Birchall/PA Wire)

In a victim personal statement, Ms Ballentyne described how she had been left with "severe anxiety" following Atticus’s death. "I will never know what kind of person Atticus would have become," she said.

She continued: "I will never see him hit milestones. I will never see him go to school. I will never see him grow up and have a family of his own."

Ms Ballentyne added: "Who plans their baby’s funeral? Who goes to the chapel of rest? I had to wait 11 hours and 18 minutes for Atticus to die. It was horrendous. I was scared to go out, I was scared to stay in.

"I don’t enjoy any moments because I have a dead son. It is mentally and emotionally draining all the time. It is awful."

Her mother, Mrs Donovan, told the court how she wondered what Atticus would look like now and what toys he would like to play with. "I just want one more day with Atticus," she said.

The grandmother continued: "I’m glad I had Atticus that night. He was loved and cuddled and had a lovely night with us. I just hope and pray he never knew what happened to him."

Representing Bartlett, Nigel Power KC said his client had previously been a "good and caring parent" to his son. "This is not a case where there is intention to kill or premeditation," Mr Power said.
